INTRODUCTION
In 1947, Congress amended the Natural Gas Act
to allow pipeline developers to acquire property
through “the right of eminent domain.” See 15 U.S.C.
§ 717f(h). Prior to this change, private companies
whose projects were approved by federal agencies had
to rely on eminent domain authority originating in
state law. And because numerous states imposed
state-specific restrictions on condemnations that were
difficult for pipeline  projects to fulfil, a federal pipe -
line permit often provided “only an illusory right to
build.” PennEast Pipeline Co. v. New Jersey, 594 U.S.
482, 489 (2021).
Pipelines were nonetheless crucial to the development of domestic energy and the integrity of American
industry. To ensure that these critical nationwide projects were not stymied by parochial  and highly vary -
ing state implementation of eminent domain, Con -
gress delegated to the pipeline companies “the federal
eminent domain power.” PennEast, 594 U.S. at 489.
Petitioners question whether state or federal law
controls the bounds of compensation to be awarded in
Natural Gas Act condemnation proceedings . But the
specific dispute in this case is limited to whether petitioners may recover “ attorney’s fees and expenses .”
Pet. App. 18a. While North Dakota authorizes awards
of attorneys’ fees in state condemnation cases, it is
well established that fees are generally unavailable
where the United States condemns property under its
own authority. In understanding the contours of the
“right of eminent domain” conferred in the Natural
Gas Act, 15 U.S.C. §  717f(h), the Eighth Circuit
turned to federal, rather than state,  law, and there -
fore held that attorney fees were unavailable.

2



That decision does not present an appropriate
candidate for certiorari, for three reasons.
First, this case is a poor vehicle for review of the
question presented , which petitioners frame as
whether “just compensation” in Natural Gas Act condemnation proceedings should “be determined by reference to state law .” Pet. i. But this case is about at -
torneys’ fees, and u nlike certain other states, North
Dakota does not define just compensation to include
those fees—it merely has a separate fee- shifting provision applicable in condemnation proceedings that
gives courts discretion  to award costs and f ees, distinct from the compensation owed for the value of the
property. Quite apart from the question of which law
governs the measure of compensation for a taking,
there is no reason to think that Congress intended for
state fee -shifting statutes to control in the federal
cause of action it created in Section 717f(h).
Second, the split on this issue —to the extent one
exists—is recent and shallow. Because the availability
of fees in North Dakota is not a question of  just compensation, the judgment below does not conflict with
cases where courts actually faced the question pre -
sented. And in any event, the Eighth Circuit is the
only appellate court to have considered the question
on a fresh slate since this Court clarified the nature of
Section 717f(h)’s delegation in PennEast . While one
other court has, in a divided ruling, declined to reconsider its pre-PennEast precedents, there is a strong
likelihood that the Eighth Circuit’s opinion could shift
the tide and bring the circuits to consensus on the correct side of this legal question. The Court should allow
the issue to further percolate in the lower courts, as
waiting may obviate the need for this Court’s review.

3



Third, the Eighth Circuit was correct on the merits. When a pipeline company condemns property under the Natural Gas Act, it is exercising the United
States’s own sovereign power of eminent domain.
More than a century of precedent carefully circum -
scribed the permissible remedies in federal condem -
nation proceedings, and had foreclosed the availabil -
ity of attorneys’ fees for decades when Congress
adopted Section 717 f(h). The provision thus contains
no gap to be filled by reference to state law. And even
if it did, the Kimbell Foods analysis demonstrates the
need for a uniform federal rule.
The petition should be denied.
STATEMENT
A. Legal background
1. Sovereign governments have possessed the
right of eminent domain for centuries, dating back to
biblical times. Abraham Bell, Private Takings, 76 U.
Chi. L. Rev. 517, 524 ( 2009) (citing 1 Samuel 8:14).
The power is so nearly an inherent aspect of sover -
eignty that it “appertains to every independent gov -
ernment.” Miss. & Rum River Boom Co. v.  Patterson,
98 U.S. 403, 406 (1878). And while “the Constitution
and Bill of Rights * * * did not include the words ‘eminent domain,’” the f ederal government has “ex -
cersi[zed] its eminent domain authority” since
“[s]hortly after the founding.” PennEast Pipeline Co.
v. New Jersey, 594 U.S. 482, 494 (2021). Because eminent domain “was one of those means well known
when the Constitution was adopted,” the federal gov -
ernment’s authority to condemn property through eminent domain “ought not to be questioned.”  Kohl v.
United States, 91 U.S. 367, 372 (1875).

4



At first, the Federal Government’s uses of emi -
nent domain were limited principally to “areas subject
to exclusive federal jurisdiction,” such as the District
of Columbia. PennEast, 594 U.S. at 494 (citing Act of
Mar. 3, 1809, 2 Stat. 539)). But within a few decades,
this Court confirmed that the United States could exercise eminent domain over property within state borders. Kohl, 91 U.S. 367. So long as “the object is within
the authority of Congress, the right to realize it
through the exercise of eminent domain is clear.” Berman v. Parker, 348 U.S. 26, 33 (1954). Exercising this
authority, the federal government has used eminent
domain “to facilitate transportation, supply water,
construct public buildings, and aid in defense readi -
ness.” Env’t & Natural Res. Div., History of the Fed -
eral Use of Eminent Domain, Dep’t of Justice (Jan. 30,
2024), perma.cc/N5XR-6B4Q. It has also condemned
property to create parks and wildlife reserves, including Rock Creek National Park. Ibid.
Just as clear as the federal government’s eminent
domain power is that Congress may exercise “its eminent domain authority through both its own officers
and private del egatees.” PennEast, 594 U.S. at 493.
“For as long as the eminent domain power has been
exercised by the United States, it has also been delegated to private parties.” Id. at 495. Such delegations
were ubiquitous among the states throughout the
nineteenth century (Bell, supra, at 545), and commonplace for the federal government. See,  e.g., Custiss v.
Georgetown & Alexandria Tpk. Co., 10 U.S. (6 Cranch)
233 (1810); California v. Cent. Pac. R.R. Co., 127 U.S.
1 (1888) ; Cherokee Nation v.  S. Kan. Rwy. Co., 135
U.S. 641 (1890);  Luxton v. N. River Bridge Co. , 153
U.S. 525, 532-534 (1894). The thrust of this consistent

5



history is that Congress “may, at its discretion, use its
sovereign powers, directly or through a corporation
* * * for the accommodation of interstate commerce.”
Luxton, 153 U.S. at 530.
When a private delegee exercises the eminent domain power, the “delegation[] essentially put[ s] the
private actor * * * in the place of the government with
regard to the law of eminent domain.” Bell, supra, at
545. Because eminent domain “is traditionally associated with sovereignty,” those wielding that power are
necessarily state actors. Jackson v. Metro. Edison Co.,
419 U.S. 345, 353 (1974). There is no such thing in our
constitutional order as a “private” use of eminent domain. When a private entity condemns land under authority granted to it by Congress, it acts “to give effect
to the federal eminent domain power.” PennEast, 594
U.S. at 502. I t is Congress condemning the property
for federal purposes, not the entity itself.
2. The Natural Gas Act (NGA) “follows this path.”
PennEast, 594 U.S. at 498. “Natural gas has been part
of the Nation’s energy supply since at least the 1820s.”
Id. at 488. As technology improved, companies began
to develop pipelines to carry natural gas across the
country. Id. at 488- 489. Congress thus enacted the
NGA in 1938 “to regulate the transportation and sale
of natural gas in interstate commerce.” Id. at 489. The
NGA gave the Federal Power Commission (now the
Federal Energy Regulatory Commission, FERC) exclusive jurisdiction to regulate the rates and facilities
of natural gas companies. Schneidewind v. ANR Pipeline Co., 485 U.S. 293, 300-301 (1988).
Before it can construct, extend, acquire, or operate
any facility for the transportation of natural gas in interstate commerce, a natural gas company must ob -

6



tain from FERC a “certificate of public convenience
and necessity.” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(c)(1)(A). A certificate
will issue only after notice and hearing, at which
members of the public and affected property -holders
may object. 15 U.S.C. § 717f(c)(1)(B). FERC will grant
the certificate only on finding the company willing and
able to complete the project in compliance with t he
provisions of the NGA and FERC’s implementing regulations, which are “extensive.” 15 U.S.C.  § 717f(e) ;
ANR Pipeline Co. , 485 U.S. at 302. FERC may also
attach “to the issuance of the certificate and to the
exercise of the rights granted thereunder such
reasonable terms and conditions as the publ ic
convenience and necessity may require.” 15 U.S.C.
§ 717f(e).
The NGA was enacted alongside the Federal
Power Act (FPA) , and the two statutes share many
parallel provisions. From its inception, the FPA has
authorized licensees to exercise “the right of eminent
domain” to acquire necessary rights -of-way for the
transmission of electric power. 16 U.S.C. § 814. The
NGA lacked such a mechanism. PennEast, 594 U.S. at
489.
Instead, companies that had obtained certificates
to build pipelines were forced to rely on state eminent
domain procedures to secure the property rights they
needed. PennEast, 594 U.S. at 489.  But those state
procedures were frequently unavailable to pipeline
companies. Some states limited eminent domain to
projects that would demonstrably benefit the states’
residents. S. Rep. No. 429, 80th Cong., at 2 (1947) (collecting cases). Pipelines, which moved natural gas
across numerous states, had difficulty satisfying that
requirement. Ibid. Other states had statutory or con -

7



stitutional provisions denying eminent domain power
to out-of-state corporations. Id. at 2-3. And still others
restricted eminent domain to corporations that dis -
tributed natural gas within the state. Ibid. Because
major pipelines had to cross numerous states, the result of the inconsistent state approaches to eminent
domain meant “that certificate holders often had only
an illusory right to build.” PennEast, 594 U.S. at 489.
Congress amended the NGA in 1947 to remedy
this problem. Rather than resorting to state eminent
domain authority, Congress provided that “any holder
of a certificate of public convenience and necessity ”
may acquire necessary property rights “ by the exer -
cise of the right of eminent domain.” 15 U.S.C.
§ 717f(h); Pub. L. No. 80-245, 61 Stat. 459 (1947). If a
certificate holder “cannot acquire by contract” or was
“unable to agree with the owner” on the appropriate
compensation for the property or right-of-way needed
for the project, the certificate holder may instit ute a
condemnation proceeding in “the district court of the
United States for the district in which such property
may be located, or in the State courts.” Ibid.
B. Factual and procedural background
1. WBI is an interstate natural gas company.
Since 1985, WBI has held a certificate of public con -
venience and necessity from FERC authorizing it to
acquire and operate interstate pipeline facilities pre -
viously owned and operated by Montana-Dakota Utilities Co. Pet. App. 28a. On November 30, 2017, WBI
filed a prior notice request for authorization to con -
struct and operate approximately 12 miles of 24- inch
diameter pipeline connecting WBI’s existing Spring
Creek Meter Station to the existing Che rry Creek
Valve Settin g, and to expand two meter stations,

8



within McKenzie County, North Dakota. Pet. App.
29a; see 82 Fed. Reg. 60 ,007 (Dec. 18, 2017). FERC
issued a notice of authorization under WBI’s existing
certificate, which was published several days later in
the Federal Register. Ibid.
WBI brought a condemnation action under Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 71.1 and Section 717f(h)
of the NGA to obtain permanent easements and tem -
porary rights -of-way over Petitioners’ property in
North Dakota. Pet. App. 28a- 29a. The district court
promptly adopted the parties’ stipulation that WBI
could immediately use and possess the easements,
leaving only the amount of compensation to be deter -
mined. Id. at 29a. The parties reached a settlement on
that question, with Petitioners reserving their right to
seek attorneys’ fees and expenses (and WBI reserving
the right to oppose). Pet. App. 29a-30a.
2. The district court  held that the availability of
attorneys’ fees to the condemnee in federal eminent
domain proceedings is determined by the law of the
state in which the condemned property is located. Pet.
App. 14a-23a.
The district court began with the premise that the
analysis where a delegee condemns property must be
“distinct, unique, and separate from circumstances in
which the United States” itself “is filling the role of
the condemner.” Pet. App. 31a. It correctly noted that
nothing in the text of Section 717f(h) required the application of state law.1 But it then concluded that Rule

1  A later clause in Section 717f(h) states that the “practice and
procedure in any action or proceeding  * * * shall conform as
nearly as may be with the practice and procedure in similar
action or proceeding in the courts of the State where the property

9



71.1 and the NGA “are silent regarding the applica -
tion of state law in condemnation proceedings under
the statute.” Id.  at 32a. And in North Dakota, the
court “may in its discretion award to the defendant
reasonable actual or statutory costs or both, which
may include * * *reasonable attorney’s fees for all ju -
dicial proceedings.” N.D.C.C. § 32 -15-32. The district
court thus endeavored to determine whether federal
or state law provided the rule of decision.
The court rejected WBI’s arguments that federal
law foreclosed the availability of attorneys’ fees. Pet.
App. 32a & n.2. It then applied the framework this
Court laid out in United States v. Kimbell Foods, Inc.,
440 U.S. 715 (1979). The court surveyed several deci -
sions by federal appellate courts. Pet. App. 35a-40a. It
concluded that there is no overriding need for a na -
tionally uniform rule . Id. at 41a-42a. The district
court then held that applying North Dakota’s fee -
shifting statute would not frustrate the NGA’s objec -
tives, and that instead a uniform federal rule would

is situated.” That language required conformity in “ procedural
matters only” ( United States v.  93.970 Acres of Land , 360 U.S.
328, 333 n.7 (1959)),  and so does not resolve the availability of
attorneys’ fees in a condemnation action. And in any event, this
clause has been superseded by what is now Rule 71.1. Ibid.; see
Advisory Committee Note to Rule 71A (1951) (rule “affords a
uniform procedure for all cases of condemnation invoking the
national power of eminent domain, and *  * * supplants all
statutes prescribing a different procedure.”); 28 U.S.C. § 2072(b)
(“All laws in conflict with [the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure]
shall be of no further force or effect after such rules have taken
effect.”). Rule 71.1 thus supplants any procedures that would
have been required by Section 717f(h).

10



upset existing commercial relationships. Id. at 43a-
44a.
Because it believed all three Kimbell Foods factors
favored state law, the district court concluded that
fees were available in the federal proceeding as an application of North Dakota’s law. Pet. App. 45a-46a.
3. The Eighth Circuit reve rsed. It began by observing that the NGA’s delegation of eminent domain
authority was “categorial.” Pet. App. 4a (quoting
PennEast, 594 U.S. at 498). As the delegee exercising
the federal government’s eminent domain power, WBI
“inherited all its rights and obligations.” Ibid. The nature of the power WBI possessed was to take property
(state or private), and the corresponding obligation
was to pay just compensation. Ibid.
The court of appeals next observed that “[j]ust
compensation” under the Fifth Amendment  “has a
well-established legal meaning.” Pet. App. 4a. The
measure of that compensation depends on the value of
the property, not the cost to the condemnee. Just
compensation under federal law thus normally excludes attorneys’ fees. Pet. App. 5a; see United States
v. Bodcaw Co., 440 U.S. 202, 203 (1979) (“[A]ttorneys’
fees and expenses are not embraced within just compensation.”) (quotation marks omitted). The only exceptions to this general rule are where Congress has provided otherwise by statute. Pet. App. 5a . Because no
exception applies here, the court concluded that the
required compensation in Section 717f(h) proceedings
does not include attorneys’ fees.
The Eighth Circuit rejected the district court’s
application of Kimbell Foods. Pt. App. 7a. While Kimbell Foods is the right analysis to fill statutory “gaps,”
“when it comes to eminent domain, congressional si -

11



lence leaves no ‘gaps’ to fill.” Ibid. The court perceived
no reason why the well- established rules concerning
just compensation should change “when the federal
government hands the keys over to a private party.”
Pet. App. 8a. It grounded its holding in this Court’s
recent decision in PennEast. There, as the Eighth Circuit explained, this Court held that “through the Natural Gas Act, the gas company received what
amounted to the entire  federal eminent -domain
power, not just some diluted form of it.” Pet. App. 8a.
Moreover, any “policy arguments” in favor of fees
are “better addressed to Congress.” Pet. App. 9a. The
Court concluded that “[t]he Fifth Amendment , not
state law or federal common law, fills any ‘gaps’ in the
Natural Gas Act.” Pet. App. 9a-10a. And fees are unavailable under the Fifth Amendment . Bodcaw, 440
U.S. at 203.
REASONS FOR DENYING THE PETITION
This case is not an appropriate candidate for re -
view, for three reasons.
First, this case does not implicate the question
presented. Because North Dakota allows for fees in
condemnation actions through a standalone fee-shifting statute rather than by incorporating fees into its
measure of just compensation, the question of “how to
determine the amount of just compensation ” (Pet. i)
does not arise, and the case is instead easily resolved
by application of the common-law American Rule.
Second, for that same reason there is no true split
over the issue in this case. To the extent the cases
cited by petitioner involved attorney fees at all (most
did not), they concerned states that—unlike North
Dakota—do count attorney’s fees in the measure of
just compensation under state law. The difference in

12



outcomes is therefore attributable to differences in the
law of the relevant states, not a split over an im -
portant federal-law question.
Moreover, even if the case were a proper vehicle
for the question presented, any split on this question
is recent and shallow. The Eighth Circuit based its
holding in large part on this Court’s recent decision in
PennEast Pipeline Co ., v. New Jersey, 594 U.S. 482
(2021). It is the only court of appeals to have con -
sidered on a clean slate whether state or federal law
defines just compensation since the Court clarified
that when Congress delegates the federal eminent domain power to a private corporation, Congress is still
“us[ing] its sovereign powers.” Id. at 496 (quoting Luxton v. N. River Bridge Co., 153 U.S. 525, 530 ( 1894)).
That PennEast led the Eighth Circuit to the correct
result here suggests that further percolation is
warranted.
And third, the Eighth Circuit was correct. There
is no gap in the NGA to be filled by state law, and even
if a gap existed , the Court’s framework mandates a
uniform federal law to govern the implementation of
the nationwide gas pipeline system, rather than a
patchwork of parochial state laws.
The petition should be denied.
A. This case does not implicate the question
presented.
Petitioners seek this Court’s review to answer
whether “just compensation” in NGA condemnation
proceedings should “be determined by reference to
state law.” Pet. i. While there are indeed cases where
that question would be outcome-determinative, this is
not one of them.

13



Petitioners admit that the dispute here is solely
over “fees and costs.” Pet. 2; see, e.g., Pet. App. 2a, 10a,
18a, 22a -23a. And all agree that attorneys’ fees are
available in condemnation proceedings in North Da -
kota courts. A state statute says so in unambiguous
terms: “The court may in its discretion award to the
defendant reasonable actual or statutory costs or
both, which may include *  * * reasonable attorney’s
fees for all judicial proceedings.” N.D.C.C. § 32-15-32.
But that law does not make those fees part  of the
measure of just compensation. Instead, North Dakota
statutes require that compensation for the use of em -
inent domain must be “ascertain[ed]” by a jury unless
waived (N.D.C.C. § 32 -15-01(2)), and provide a list of
the categories of compensation that the  jury may
award (id. § 32-15-22). That list does not include at -
torneys’ fees, which are instead governed by the separate statutory provision just cited. And that separate
fee-shifting provision merely permits “the court” (not
the jury that must determine just compensation ) to
shift fees “in its discretion” ( id. § 32 -15-32)—which
discretion would be impermissible if fees were actu -
ally part of the “just compensation” guaranteed to
property owners by the state constitution. See N.D.
Const. Art. 1, § 16.
This structure is different from the mechanisms
employed by some other states , which have made attorneys’ fees part of their  constitutional standards of
just compensation. See,  e.g., Joseph B. Doerr Tr. v.
Cent. Fla. Expressway Auth. , 177 So.3d 1209, 1215
(Fla. 2015) (“[F]ull compensation under the Florida
Constitution includes the right to a reasonable attor -
ney’s fee for the property owner.”) ; Keeton v. Alaska,
441 P.3d 933, 939 (Alaska 2019) (“[P]ayment to a con-

14



demnee of n ecessary appraiser’s and attorney’s fees”
is required under “the just compensation principle of
the Alaska Constitution.”) (quotation marks omitted).
North Dakota’s choice to make attorneys’ fees discretionary, rather than to guarantee them as part of
just compensation, is, of course, a permissible one .
Property owners are entitled under the Fourteenth
Amendment to a minimum “just compensation” in
state condemnation proceedings. Dohany v. Rogers,
281 U.S. 362, 366 (1930). But “[a]ttorneys’ fees and
expenses are not embraced within just compensation”
for purposes of determining whether state procedures
offend the federal Constitution. Id. at 368. Thus, “[a]
state may allow the recovery of an attorney’s fee in
special classes of [condemnation] proceedings while
withholding them in others”—or, it may constitutionally deny recovery of fees altogether.  Ibid. That decision is ultimately one of policy left to state legisla -
tures.
By contrast, Congress has chosen not to authorize
fee shifting in Section 717f(h) actions. When Congress
created the condemnation cause of action at issue here
and provided district courts with jurisdiction, it was
silent as to the availability of fees. But the “‘basic
point of reference’ when considering the award of at -
torney’s fees is the bedrock principle known as the
‘American Rule.’” Hardt v. Reliance Standard Life Ins.
Co., 560 U.S. 242, 252 -253 (2010) (quoting Ruckel -
shaus v. Sierra Club, 463 U.S. 680, 683 (1983)). In the
federal system, “[e]ach li tigant pays his own attor -
ney’s fees, win or lose, unless a statute or contract provides otherwise.” Ibid.
The distinction between fees included in just compensation and fees awarded once just compensation

15



has been determined is especially clear in condemna -
tion proceedings initiated by the federal government
itself. There is no dispute that fees are excluded from
the measure of just compensation in such cases. Bod -
caw, 440 U.S. at  203; Pet. 18. But fees are, in some
cases, nonetheless available. The Equal Access to Justice Act allows an award of fees to the prevailing party
in litigation brought by or against the United States.
28 U.S.C. § 2412(b). This rule applies in eminent do -
main cases—the statute contains an express mathe -
matical definition for determining the “prevailing
party” in “the case of eminent domain proceedings.”
28 U.S.C. § 2412(d)(2)(H).
Fees can thus be available either as a matter of
just compensation or by separate legislative proviso.
This case turns not on whether North Dakota law re -
quires fees in its constitutional definition of just compensation—it does not 2—but on simple question
whether North Dakota’s fee shifting provision applies

2  The Eighth Circuit cited (at Pet. App. 3a) Petersburg Sch. Dist.
of Nelson Cnty. v.  Peterson, 103 N.W. 756, 759 (N.D. 1905), for
the proposition that the North Dakota constitution incorporates
fees into just compensation. But that case discusses only “taxable
costs” (ibid.) which are by definition those costs that do not
require a separate award. See Cost, Black’s Law Dictionary (12th
ed. 2024). U nder the American Rule, taxable costs do not
ordinarily include attorneys’ fees in the absence of a contrary
statute, and the same is true in North Dakota. See N.D. R. Civ.
P. 54(e) (distinguishing between taxable “costs” and “attorneys’
fees and related nontaxable expenses”). That is presumably why
North Dakota enacted N.D.C.C. § 32-15-32 in the first place. And
if Petersburg School District  really meant that all costs were
constitutionally guaranteed, that would render Section 32-15-
32—which makes them discretionary —unconstitutional. See
page 13, supra.

16



to a federal cause of action that does not provide for
fee shifting itself.
The answer to that simple question is a simple
“No.” While state rules of decision may apply in diversity cases, jurisdiction in Section 717f(h) cases is pro -
vided for by Section 717f(h) itself and, potentially, 28
U.S.C. § 1331. I n such cases, “[w]hat Congress has
done * * * while fully recognizing and accepting the
general rule, is to make specific and explicit provi -
sions for the allowance of attorneys’ fees under se -
lected statutes granting or protecting various federal
rights.” Alyeska Pipeline Serv. Co. v. Wilderness Soc’y,
421 U.S. 240, 260 (1975). Federal courts may depart
from the American Rule only if “there is express statutory authorization to the contrary.” Hensley v. Eckerhart, 461 U.S. 424, 429 (1983); accord  Lackey v.
Stinnie, 145 S. Ct. 659, 666 (2025). And where federal
common law (like the American Rule) already exists,
the Court has rejected arguments that state law
should provide the rule of decision. See,  e.g., California ex rel. State Lands Comm’n v.  United States, 457
U.S. 273, 284 (1982).
Indeed, Congress has spoken to the issue of attorneys’ fees in condemnation proceedings. In 1987, Congress amended the Uniform Relocation  Assistance
and Real Property Acquisition Policies  Act (URA) to
define “Federal agency” to include “any person who
has the authority to acquire property by eminent do -
main under Federal law.” Pub. L. No. 100 -17, § 401,
101 Stat. 132, 246; see 42 U.S.C. § 4601(1). And “person” means “any individual, partnership, corporation,
or association.” 42 U.S.C § 4601(5). The Relocation Act
provides for awards of attorneys’ fees in two narrow
classes of condemnation proceedings:  if “the final

17



judgment is that the Federal agency cannot acquire
the real property by condemnation;” or “the proceed -
ing is abandoned by the United States.” 4 2 U.S.C.
§ 4654(a). Courts have applied this provision in NGA
proceedings. See,  e.g., Transwestern Pipeline Co. v.
17.19 Acres of Prop. Located in Maricopa Cnty. , 627
F.3d 1268 (9th Cir. 2010). It is undisputed that this
case does not match either scenario , making fees
unavailable under federal law. Pet. App. 5a. It is thus
implausible that Congress intended the availability of
fees to be governed by state law.
Given that Congress did not provide for fee shift -
ing, fees are unavailable as a matter of federal law.
And because fees are available in North Dakota con -
demnation proceedings only through a statutory fee
shifting mechanism (as opposed to inclusion within
just compensation itself , as in certain other states ),
the measure of just compensation has no relevance to
the availability of fees under Section 717f(h)  in this
case. This case therefore is not a proper vehicle for the
Court to consider the question presented.
B. There is no split warranting this Court’s
review.
1. As just discussed, this case does not implicate
the question presented. For the same reason, it does
not conflict with the cases identified in the Petition.3
Petitioners rely heavily on the Third Circuit’s
opinion in Tennessee Gas Pipeline Co. v.  Permanent
Easement for 7.053 Acres, 931 F.3d 237 (3d Cir. 2019).

Indeed, it is a clear example of an attorneys’ fees case

Finally, the Eleventh Circuit’s holding in Sabal

In sum, Petitioners have identified several cases

But, because it is not relevant on the facts of this case,
the Eighth Circuit’s judgment does not conflict with
those decisions. Cf., e.g., William Baude, The Judg -
ment Power, 96 Geo. L.J. 1807, 1844 (2008)  (“ Judgments become binding law, not opinions.”).
2. Even if this case did turn on whether federal or
state law controlled the definition of just compensa -

tion in Section 717f(h) proceedings, this Court’s re -

Cir. 2023) (Grant, J., concurring) (“ Like at least one

Because so few courts have addressed the ques -
tion presented in the years since PennEast, there have
been few opportunities to assess how courts will react
to and apply the Court’s opinion. Percolation following
PennEast is thus warranted.
C. The decision below is correct.
The Eighth Circuit’s holding that fees are unavailable in S ection 717f(h) proceedings is correct as a
straightforward application of the American Rule. Supra, pages 14-17. But even if North Dakota did define
just compensation to include attorneys’ fees—again, it
does not —the holding below would still be correct.
Because it is Congress exercising its sovereign
eminent domain power even when that power is delegated to natural gas companies, the federal rule that
fees are excluded from just compensation controls.
And, though a Kimbell Foods analysis is unnecessary,
the NGA has all the hallmarks of a context in which a
uniform federal rule is required.
1. Attorneys’ fees are unavailable in
federal condemnation proceedings
regardless of delegations.
a. The Natural Gas Act allows certificate holders
like WBI to “exercise * * * the right of eminent do -
main.” 15 U.S.C. § 717f(h). As this Court recently ex -
plained, that delegation is “categorical.” PennEast,
594 U.S. at 498. And when a private delegee con -
demns land, it is “the Federal Government” that is
“exercis[ing] its eminent domain authority.” Id.  at
493. The Court has long recognized that Congress
“may, at its discretion, use its sovereign powers * * *

22



through a corporation ,” as an alternative to doing so
“directly.” Luxton, 153 U.S. at 530; see PennEast, 594
U.S. at 495 (“For as long as the eminent domain power
has been exercised by the United States, it has also
been delegated to private parties.”).
Because Congress has two equivalent paths
through which it can permissibly exercise its sovereign eminent domain power, this Court has found no
cause to differentiate between condemnations by the
federal government and those by its delegees. In
PennEast, the Court held that private delegee’s
“condemnation action to give effect to the federal
eminent do main power falls comfortably within the
class of suits to which States consented under the plan
of the Con vention.” 594 U.S. at 50 2. It further
explained that the Eleventh Amendment —which
ordinarily would bar almost any  suit by a private
party against a nonconsenting state—is no obstacle to
delegees’ condemna tion suits against states. Id.  at
506. A delegee exercis ing eminent domain simply
stands in the shoes of the federal government, and its
rights and obligations are no more and no less than
those of the federal govern ment in an identical
proceeding.
Indeed, there is no rational basis for any substantive distinction between condemnation proceedings
captioned “United States” and proceedings initiated
by a delegee. Nobody disputes that Congress could
have created a nearly identical statutory scheme in
which pipeline companies apply to FERC when they
are unable to obtain rights-of-way for FERC-approved
projects and then FERC itself condemns the property
and transfers the right to the company. In delegating
authority to pipeline companies directly, Congres s

23



merely chose between one of two permissible but in -
terchangeable paths to exercise its own sovereign authority. PennEast, 594 U.S. at 498.  A distinction be -
tween the two options thus “has no basis—the choice
of how to exercise the eminent domain power and
what additional compensation to provide belongs to
Congress alone.” Sabal Trail, 74 F.4th at 1350 (Grant,
J., concurring); accord Sabal Trail, 59 F.4th at 1175
(Jordan, J., concur ring); Tennessee Gas Pipeline Co. ,
931 F.3d at 257 (Chagares, J., dissenting);  Georgia
Power, 617 F.2d at 1129 (Rubin, J., dissenting).
b. Just compensation under the Fifth Amendment
does not include attorneys’ fees. The proper measure
of just compensation is the “full monetary equivalent
of the property taken.” Almota Farmers Elevator &
Warehouse Co. v.  United States , 409 U.S. 470, 473
(1973). The Court has never “deviated” from the principle that “just compensation ‘is for the property, and
not to the owner.’” Bodcaw , 440 U.S at 203 (quoting
Monongahela Nav. Co. v. United States, 148 U.S. 312,
326 (1893)). Thus, the Court has consistently rejected
arguments that the c onstitutional min imum should
reach “indirect costs” like “attorneys’ fees.” Ibid.
The federal measure of just compensation applies
in any proceeding where the “substantive right” to
compensation is “grounded upon the Constitution of
the United States.” United States v.  Miller, 317 U.S.
369, 379- 380 (1943) ; accord Kohl, 91 U.S. at 372
“[W]here essential interests of the Federal Govern -
ment are concerned, federal law rules unless Congress
chooses to make state laws applicable.” United States
v. 93.970 Acres of Land, 360 U.S. 328, 332-333 (1959).
A property owner’s right to compensation in a
Section 717f(h) condemnation originates in the Fifth

24



Amendment. The NGA does not mention “just com -
pensation,” or provide that compensation must be
paid for taken property at all. 15 U.S.C. § 717f(h). The
obligation to pay comes from the delegation of the federal “eminent domain” power, which is bounded by the
federal constitutional minimum of just compensation.
Ibid.
That is, because a pipeline company exercises a
categorical delegation of the federal eminent domain
power, the substantive right to compensation is trig -
gered by an exercise of federal authority. And that federal authority implicates federal constitutional pro -
tections. Kirby Forest Indus., Inc. v.  United States ,
467 U.S. 1, 9 (1984). Miller thus instructs that the federal measure of just compensation applies. 317 U.S. at
380. There is simply no gap to be filled by state law ,
as the contours of the federal eminent domain power
“can neither be enlarged nor diminished by a State.”
Kohl, 91 U.S. at 374.
c. Other considerations reinforce the conclusion
that Congress left no gap to be filled by reference to
state law.
First, Congress has in fact spoken to the availability of attorneys’ fees in condemnation proceedings
brought by private delegees. The URA allows fees in a
narrow set of circumstances where federal agencies—
defined to include private delegees —exercise the federal eminent domain authority to condemn property.
42 U.S.C. §§ 4601(1), 4654(a). That provision applies
to NGA proceedings. Transwestern Pipeline Co. , 627
F.3d 1268.  But it does not apply here,  because this
case meets neither of the defined fact patt erns in
which fee shifting is available  as an exception to the
American Rule. Pet. App. 5a. That fees are unavaila-

25



ble under this provision is a function of Congress’s explicit policy decisions, not of its silence —leaving no
room for state law. See, e.g., United States v. Johnson,
529 U.S. 53, 58 (2000) (“When Congress provides ex -
ceptions in a statute * * * [t]he proper inference” * * *
is that Congress considered the issue of exceptions
and, in the end, limited the statute to the ones set
forth.”).
Second, the unavailability of fees is underscored
by inclusion of relevant language in other, related
statutes—including other provisions of the NGA. The
General Bridge Act, for example, requires compensa -
tion to be “ascertained and paid according to the laws
of [the] State” in which the condemnation occurs, in -
cluding attorneys’ fees where available under state
law. 33 U.S.C. § 532. And the NGA itself elsewhere is
explicit where it permits deviation from the federal
standard for just compensation. See 15 U .S.C.
§§ 717y(b)(2), (e)(2)- (3). These provisions show that
where Congress intends to depart from the federal
standard, “it has done so clearly and expressly.” FCC
v. NextWave Pers. Commc’ns, Inc. , 537 U.S. 293, 302
(2003).
Third, the context in which Congress enacted Section 717f(h) strongly suggests that Congress intended
matters of substance to be governed by federal, rather
than state, law. “No one disputes that § 717f(h) was
passed specifically to solve the problem of States im -
peding interstate pipeline development” through
“their own eminent domain” laws. PennEast, 594 U.S.
at 498. To solve this problem, Congress delegated the
entirety of its eminent domain authority to pipeline
companies. Doing so provided pipeline companies an
efficient path around restrictive state eminent domain

26



procedures. It is implausible that in solving this
problem Congress intended to nonetheless allow
disuniformity on  a substantive matter as critical as
how to measure compensation.
Indeed, Congress did express that state law
should still control some aspects of Section 717f(h)
condemnations. That language adopted state law as
to “procedural matters only.” 93.970 Acres, 360 U.S. at
333 n.7. The measure of compensation is substantive,
not procedural. Miller , 317 U.S. at 380 ( explaining
that “the measure of compensation” is a “question[] of
substantive right”). That Congress specified state law
should apply to one set of questions strongly implies
its intent that state law not  govern questions outside
the specified category. See, e.g., NLRB v. SW. Gen.,
Inc., 580 U.S. 288, 302 (2017) (“[E]xpressing one item
of an associated group or series excludes another left
unmentioned.”).
Together, these considerations lead to the ines -
capable conclusion that Congress designed Section
717f(h) to categorically delegate the federal eminent
domain power, and in doing so to incorporate the
standards applicable to exercises of the federal emi -
nent domain power. That choice leaves no gap to be
filled by state law or federal common law—the inquiry
ought to end here.
d. Petitioners’ arguments to the contrary are unconvincing.
First, Petitioners invoke a general rule that delegations of eminent domain “must be construed strictly
against the grantee.” Pet. 15 (quoting 1A Nichols on
Eminent Domain  § 3.03(6)(b) (3d ed. 2018)).  True,
some delegations “are, in their very nature, grants of
limited powers *  * * [and] do not include sovereign

27



powers greater than those expressed or necessarily
implied.” United States v. Carmack, 329 U.S. 230, 243
n.13 (1946). But Petitioners’ argument on this score
completely disregards this Court’s holding in Penn -
East that the delegation in Section 717f(h) is “categorical.” 594 U.S. at 498. There is no need to resort to
background presumptions (even if those presump -
tions retain any validity) in the face of a clear, total
delegation of the federal eminent domain power.
Second, Petitioners invoke Section 717f(h)’s defunct “practice and procedure” language. Pet. 16. But
that language undermines rather than supports Petitioners’ argument. It applies to “procedural matters
only,” and does not cover matters of substance like the
measure of compensation. 93.970 Acres, 360 U.S. at
333 n.7; see supra pages 8-9 & n.1. The provision was
presumably necessary because, in 1947, there was not
yet a uniform set of federal procedures to govern con -
demnation proceedings —Rule 71.1 was adopted in
1951—and Congress did not want to take on the pro -
ject of crafting one in its narrow attempt to fix an
omission in the NGA. By specifying that state law governs procedure (a requirement superseded by Rule
71.1), Congress i mplied that substantive matters
would not be governed by state law. There is nothing
counterintuitive about that.
Third, Petitioners misunderstand the history of
the federal eminent domain power. Pet. 16. Contrary
to Petitioners’ telling, the federal government has exercised the federal  eminent domain power since
“[s]hortly after the founding.” PennEast , 594 U.S. at
494. For more than fifty years before Congress en -
acted Section 717f(h), the Court had  thus held that
“the exercise of the federal eminent domain power was

28



a means that was ‘known and appropriate’ at the time
of the founding.” Id. at 505 (quoting Kohl , 91 U.S. at
372). There was therefore a century and a half of precedent defining the contours of the federal eminent domain power when Congress amended the NGA in
1947. Petitioners’ suggestion that Congress in 1947
would have hesitated to rely on this body of law because the federal government had also relied on state
eminent domain proceedings in the first half of the
nineteenth century is puzzling.
Fourth, Petitioners argue (at 16- 17) that Con -
gress legislates against “the general rule” that state
law ought to govern the availability of fees. They have
the law backwards. Congress legislates against the
backdrop of the well -established “American Rule,”
which states that fee shifting is generally unavailable
unless Congress specifies otherwise. See supra pages
14-17. Congressional silence on fee shifting is thus not
an attempt to rely on state law; it is a determina tion
that fees are unavailable as a matter of federal law.6

6  Petitioners further suggest (at 17) that the Eighth Circuit’s
rule would render superfluous a sub -provision of the Federal
Power Act that was added in 2005 and specifies a fair -marketvalue measure of just compensation . See 16 U.S.C. § 824p(f) (2).
But legislation frequently involves redundancy and surplusage
for the purpose of clarity. See, e.g., Marx v. Gen. Revenue Corp.,
568 U.S. 371, 385 (2013) . And that conclusion is especially
justified when related provisions are undoubtedly superfluous .
Ibid. That is just the case here: The neighboring subsection (f)(1),
which provides that “[a]ny right -of-way acquired pursuant to
subsection (e) shall be considered a taking of private property,”
is superfluous under any reading, since “the exercise of eminent
domain” (16 U.S.C. § 824p(e)) constitutes a Fifth Amendment
taking regardless of whether a statute says so . Because
subsection (f)(1) is obviously superfluous, the implication is that

29



Finally, Petitioners insist that there are crucial
differences between cases where Congress exercises
its eminent domain authority and those in which it
exercises the authority through a private delegee.
They fail, however, to explain what those differences
actually are. But “[s]ince the founding, the Federal
Government has exercised its eminent domain
authority through both its own officers and private
delegatees.” PennEast, 594 U.S. at 493. In either case,
it is the federal government exercising its authority—
the choice of mechanism belongs to Congress alone.
There is no reason to impose distinctions between
applicable law where Congress has not chosen to do
so.
2. Even under Kimbell Foods,
compensation in federal condemnation
proceedings should be governed by
federal law.
Petitioners attack the Eighth Circuit ’s holding
that federal law governs the measure of just compen -
sation, but the Petition notably omits the analysis this
Court has required to govern choice -of-law questions
where Congress leaves gaps in statutes. Though there
is no gap to fill here, a n application of the Kimbel
Foods framework shows that federal law should con -
trol even if there were. United States v. Kimbell Foods,
Inc., 440 U.S. 715 (1979).
First, there is a need for a uniform federal rule to
govern the measure of compensation in NGA condemnations. Kimbell Foods , 440 U.S. at 728. Section

Congress here was legislating for clarity rather than
independent effect, and the Court should “not [be] overly
concerned” if subsection (f)(2) “may be redundant as well.” Marx,
568 U.S. at 385.

30



717f(h) was enacted precisely to remedy systemic
problems arising from such a lack of uniformity. Penn-
East, 594 U.S. at 498; S. Rep. No. 429, at 2-4. Prior to
the 1947 amendments, states were able to erect barriers to favor parochial interests over critical nation -
wide infrastructure projects. Congress fixed this problem by enacting a “categorical” delegation of the fed -
eral eminent domain power. PennEast , 594 U.S. at
498. That delegation swept away state restrictions on
the availability of eminent domain. There is no reason
to suspect that Congress would have nevertheless
sought to maintain state valuation requirements,
which could create sufficient legal friction and in -
crease costs such that projects would be frustrated.
Petitioners (citing the Third Circuit) appear to
acknowledge that “‘crazy state laws’ might require so
much compensation that pipeline construction would
grind to a halt.” Pet. 7. That admission is dispositive.
The choice-of-law rule that governs here will be agnostic as to the substance of state law in future cases—
there is no room in Kimbell Foods to determine the
wisdom or reasonableness of state law in determining
what law applies. If there could exist future state laws
that would frustrate the federal program embodied in
the NGA, then the first factor cuts strongly in favor of
a uniform federal rule.
All this is just as applicable to the narrower question of attorneys’ fees under Section 717f(h). Congress
addressed fees in condemnation proceedings, including those initiated by private delegees, in the Uniform
Relocation Assistance and Real Property Acquisition
Policies Act. 42 U.S.C. § 4654. The URA specifies that
Congress intended to “assure consistent treatment for
owners in the many Federal programs.” 42 U.S.C.

31



§ 4651. Congress has thus adjudged the fee issue also
worthy of national consistency.
Second, reliance on state law would frustrate
congressional objectives. Kimbell Foods , 440 U.S. at
728. Congress has expressed a need for “consistent
treatment for owners” in the URA. 42 U.S.C. § 4651.
And the NGA was “framed as to afford consumers a
complete, permanent and effective bond of protection
from excessive rates and charges.” Sunray Mid -Con.
Oil Co. v. FPC, 364 U.S. 137, 147 (1960). Beyond the
inconsistency inherent in reliance on state compensation law, increased pipeline construction costs will result in higher rates for consumers.
Third, use of a uniform federal standard would
not disrupt commercial relationships based on state
law. Kimbell Foods, 440 U.S. at 728-729. There exists
“an established body of federal law on the issue of just
compensation.” Georgia Power, 617 F.3d at 1123 n.17.
There is no dispute that the federal government itself
could condemn the same easement at issue here for
the same federal purposes. And if it did so, there can
be no doubt that federal law would control. Commer -
cial relationships and expectations are formed against
the backdrop of that possibility. That Congress exer -
cises its acknowledged authority though a delegee
(also a well-established practice) is immaterial.
All three Kimbell Foods factors therefore cut in favor of federal law . As a result, the Eighth Circuit’s
holding would be correct even if there were a gap in
the NGA—which there is not.
CONCLUSION
The petition should be denied.
